What you deliberately did not do: identify the biter (their privacy is not yours to trade for peace), apologize for the other family's child, or narrate your supervision in a way that sounds like a legal defense. Under time pressure the temptation is to explain the system; the parent needs exactly three things — her child is okay, it is being handled, she has a channel tomorrow. Ninety seconds spent on those is a complete explanation. The line behind you matters too: end by moving — "walk with me to the gate" converts a queue-side confrontation into a conversation already concluding.
My director stops me in the corridor and asks 'how's the project?' I always ramble and she walks away looking worried. Give me a structure.

Three sentences, in this order: status, change, need. "We're on track for the June launch. The vendor delay cost us a week, which we've absorbed by moving the training sessions earlier. The one thing I need from you is a decision on the contractor budget by Friday, or the schedule slips."

Corridor updates fail in two opposite ways: the data dump (everything you did this week, unsorted) and the reassurance fog ("fine, fine, all good") that a director correctly reads as concealment. The three-sentence form avoids both because each sentence has a job. Status answers the question asked. Change shows you are tracking reality rather than reciting the plan — one honest complication, already handled, is the strongest credibility signal in the form. Need converts the encounter into action and, crucially, attaches a date to the consequence, which is what gets decisions made.

Prepare it before you need it: once a week, write your three sentences in your notebook. Corridor questions are not interruptions of the work of managing a project; in most organizations they are the work, because they're where your project's reputation is set.
I run a bakery and the city is closing our street for two months of roadworks. A local reporter wants a quote. I don't want to sound whiny or doomed. Help me give her the sentence.

Give her this: "We're a destination for some customers and a habit for most — and habits need a street they can park on. We'll survive it if our regulars know we're open, so that's the message: we're open, the side-street parking behind the pharmacy is free, and the coffee is on us for anyone who walked the long way round."

Anatomy of why it works in print: the first clause gives the reporter an idea she can build the story around (habit businesses versus destination businesses — she will reuse it, and your bakery becomes her example of it). The rest converts complaint into information her readers can act on: open, where to park, a small generous offer. Nothing in it begs, and nothing in it predicts doom, so it can't be cut into either.

The general rule for talking to journalists as a small business: reporters need a quotable sentence plus usable facts, and they will take both from whoever provides them most cleanly. If you don't supply the sentence, the story's sentence will be supplied by the works department. Arrive with yours written down. There is no shame in reading it — journalists prefer a considered sentence to a spontaneous paragraph they have to mine.
I work an airline gate desk. A flight just cancelled and 140 people are looking at me. I have to explain a crew timeout, which sounds like a fake excuse. Give me the announcement.

"Folks, here's exactly what happened. Your crew flew in from Denver, and by law their working day has a hard limit — it exists so that no pilot is flying tired. The Denver delay used up the last of their legal hours, so this crew cannot legally take you to Chicago tonight, and there isn't a spare crew based here. I know 'the crew timed out' sounds like a excuse invented at a desk. It's a federal safety rule, and honestly, it's one you want enforced on the days when it's inconvenient — especially on those days."

Then pivot immediately to the only thing the crowd can use: "Here's what happens now. Rebooking is automatic — check the app in the next ten minutes. If tonight doesn't work, the desk to my left is issuing hotel and meal vouchers. I will stay at this desk until the last person has a plan."

The announcement works because it converts a suspicious phrase into a rule with a reason, and it recruits the passengers' own safety instinct as your ally rather than fighting it. But note the proportion: the explanation is the smaller half. Under pressure, audiences forgive almost any cause if the next steps are concrete and a human visibly remains. Endless explanation with no vouchers is what actually enrages a gate area.
I'm a public health nurse with a 20-second radio slot about a boil-water notice. Twenty seconds. What do I say?

Twenty seconds is about fifty words, and every one must either instruct or prevent a mistake: "This is the county health department. If you live in the Riverside district, boil your tap water for one full minute before drinking, cooking, or brushing teeth, until we announce otherwise. Bottled water is fine. Ice made since yesterday should be thrown out. We'll update this station at noon and six."

What got cut, deliberately: the cause (a main break — interesting, useless), the organism names (frightening, useless), and the apology (radio listeners forgive agencies that instruct them clearly). What stayed: who is speaking (authority in four words), who is affected (a named district, so the rest of the county can stop listening), the action with its number (one full minute — the detail people actually get wrong), the edge cases that generate phone calls (bottled water, the ice already in the freezer), and when the next information arrives.

That last element is the one amateurs omit and professionals never do. A notice that doesn't say when the next update comes forces every listener to guess, and guessing people call, hoard water, or ignore the next notice. Twenty seconds bought the public's calm for six hours — that was the real product.
My neighbor is angry about noise from our home renovation. I need to explain what's happening and keep the peace. Give me what to say at his door.

Bring information, a schedule, and one concession — in that order. "Thanks for coming over instead of just stewing — I mean that. Here's where we are: the loud part is the framing, and it runs this week and next, weekdays only, and the crew starts at eight, not seven, from tomorrow. After the framing, it's interior work — drywall and floors — which you'll barely hear. If there's ever a day that's unbearable, text me and we'll shift the noisiest work to the afternoon. My number's on this card."

Three moves to notice. You thanked him for the complaint itself, which reframes him from adversary to informant — he did, in fact, do you a favor versus calling the city first. You gave the noise an end date and a daily shape, because unexplained noise is experienced as endless noise; the same decibels with a calendar attached are measurably more tolerable. And you conceded the one thing that costs little and signals everything: the start time. A concession offered before it's demanded reads as character; the same concession extracted reads as defeat, and neighbors remember which one it was when the next dispute arrives.
Mid-pitch, an investor asked me: 'Why hasn't the big incumbent just crushed you?' I froze. What's the honest short answer for next time?

The answer that works is a mechanism, not a boast: "Because our customers are too small for their sales model. Their reps need six-figure contracts to hit quota; our clinics pay four figures a year. They'd have to rebuild their pricing, their sales team, and their support to chase us, and every step down-market cannibalizes the business that pays them. They will eventually — through acquisition, probably, possibly of us. Our job is to be the expensive acquisition rather than the free copy, which is why we're focused on renewal rates in a niche they can't serve profitably."

Why the freeze happened: the question is a trap with two losing exits — bravado ("they can't touch our technology") invites demolition, and modesty ("we're lucky so far") confirms the fear. The mechanism answer escapes sideways: it concedes the incumbent's strength, explains the structural reason it doesn't apply, and — the move that separates founders who get second meetings — names the real endgame honestly, including being acquired. An investor who hears you describe your own moat's expiry date trusts your description of everything else. Prepare this answer in writing before your next pitch. The questions that freeze founders are a known, finite set; there is no excuse for meeting one unprepared twice.
I'm a pharmacist and there's a 25-minute wait. Customers keep asking 'how long can it take to put pills in a bottle?' I need a 15-second answer that doesn't sound like a corporate script.

"Fair question — the counting is the fast part. Before your bottle, I'm checking this prescription against your other six medications for interactions, and verifying the dose with your file. That check is the job, and it's the part I can't rush. You're third in line — about twenty minutes, and I'll call your name the moment it's ready."

Why it doesn't sound scripted: it concedes the visible part of the job completely ("the counting is fast") instead of defending it, which is what corporate scripts do and why everyone hates them. Then it reveals the invisible part in one concrete image — six other medications — that the customer can verify against their own knowledge of their pill organizer. And it ends with a personal queue position and an honest number rather than "we're doing our best."

The deeper principle for any craft with invisible safety work: the customer isn't wrong about what they see; they're missing what they can't. Your fifteen seconds aren't for defending the wait — they're for making the check visible once, so the wait changes meaning from idleness to diligence. Say it warmly, at eye level, not through the glass while counting. The same words delivered mid-count sound like a brush-off; delivered standing still, they sound like respect.
I'm a football coach and I have to explain at the press conference why I punted on fourth-and-short in the fourth quarter. The fans think I chickened out. Give me the explanation.

"I understand the frustration — I wanted those two yards too. Here's the arithmetic I had. We were up four, on our own forty, with six minutes left. Make it, and we can nearly run out the clock. Miss it, and they take over forty yards from tying the game with a field goal or beating us with one drive. Our punt put them on their fifteen. Their offense had scored once in the second half. I chose to make them drive eighty-five yards against the unit that had stopped them all night, rather than hand them a short field on one play. If we were behind, I go for it — the math flips. Tonight the lead was the asset, and I protected it."

Notice the explanation never says "trust me" or "that's football." It shows the decision as a comparison between two named futures, with the field positions and clock doing the arguing, and it states the condition under which you'd choose differently — which proves the choice was a calculation rather than a temperament. Fans can disagree with arithmetic; what enrages them is suspected cowardice, and a coach who shows the numbers is visibly not hiding. Also concede the emotion in the first sentence. A press conference is an explanation under pressure, and the pressure is partly grief — acknowledge it before you out-argue it.
I'm a doctor and many of my consultations happen through an interpreter. Patients end up talking to the interpreter instead of me and I lose the thread. How should I run the explanation?

Restructure around three disciplines. First, speak to the patient, always — eye contact with them, second person, short complete thoughts: "I found the cause of the pain. It is an infection, not a tumor. The medicine will treat it, and you should feel better in three days." Short segments let the interpreter render faithfully instead of summarizing, and summarizing is where nuance — and sometimes whole sentences — quietly die.

Second, brief the interpreter before the patient enters: the diagnosis, the plan, and the one sentence that must land exactly (usually the safety instruction: "come back the same day if the fever passes 39"). Professional interpreters welcome this; it converts them from a channel into a colleague with the map.

Third, verify by teach-back through the interpreter: "Tell me, in your own words, how you will take this medicine." Watch the patient's answer length — a long answer rendered as "yes, she understands" is a red flag you can act on kindly. And never let a family member, above all a child, interpret bad news or consent discussions: they will edit out of love, and you will never know which sentence they softened.

A family just moved to our country and I'm their neighbor. They need to register their address and get a driving license and it's all baffling. How do I explain bureaucracy to a newcomer without overwhelming them?

Explain the logic before the steps, because newcomers drown in steps when the logic is invisible. "Here, the system runs on one idea: the address registration is the key that opens every other door. Once the city has you registered at your address, the tax number comes by post automatically, the license office can process you, the school can enroll the kids. So we do things in the order the key unlocks them — registration first, everything else after — and each office visit produces one paper that the next office will ask for. Keep every paper in one folder, forever."

Then give them the sequence as a story of visits, not a list of agencies: which door, what to bring, what paper comes home, what it unlocks next. Add the two cultural translations that matter most: that appointments are real and lateness is costly here, and that a stamped paper outranks a friendly promise — if an official says something helpful, asking "could I have that in writing?" is normal, not rude.

Resist explaining the whole system. A newcomer needs the next two doors and the master key idea; the rest can be learned when it's their turn to need it. Bureaucracy explained all at once is a fog. Explained as a chain of unlocks, it's almost a game — and your neighbors get to feel progress after every visit instead of confusion after every form.
My grandfather was a blacksmith and he's 90. His great-grandkids think he 'made horseshoes.' I want to help him explain the trade before it's lost. What should he actually tell them?

Have him explain it as a world, not a task list, and start with the sentence that reframes everything: "Before engines, everything that moved, cut, lifted, or held together passed through a forge. I didn't make horseshoes. I made the town's tools — and when anything iron broke, from a plow to a gate hinge to a wagon axle, it came to me, because there was no shop to buy a new one."

Then have him teach with his hands and one object: a single horseshoe, passed around, while he explains how you read steel by its color — cherry red, orange, near-white — the way a cook reads a pan. Kids remember what they held. Add the economics they never guess: the smith knew everyone's business, because everyone's broken tools told him what they were planting, building, and hauling.

Record it. Not as an interview with questions, but ask him to teach one thing per sitting — how you'd shoe a difficult horse, how you knew a weld would hold — because teaching preserves what reminiscing doesn't: the judgments. His knowledge is a library that exists in exactly one copy. The explanation you're helping him build isn't for the children's information; it's the transfer itself, and it should be treated with that urgency and that honor.
My grandmother was a telephone switchboard operator in the 1950s. At a family lunch the kids asked what that even means. Give her the explanation.

She can say: "When I started, telephones couldn't call each other by themselves. If you picked up your phone, you got me. I'd say 'number, please,' and you'd tell me who you wanted. Then I took a cord — a real cord, on a board full of holes — and plugged your line into their line with my hands. Every call in town passed through my hands and my memory. I knew whose baby was coming, whose shop was busy, who shouldn't be disturbed — and a good operator forgot everything she heard, on purpose."

The cord is the detail that makes it real for children raised on invisible connections: the internet of 1955 was a woman with two hands and forty cords, and call speed was her skill. The last sentence is the one the adults at the table will remember — the operator's professional discretion, the ethics of a human switchboard. If the kids ask one follow-up, it's usually "what if two people called at once?" — and she'll be off, describing the board lighting up at Christmas. Give her the opening; the trade will explain itself from there, in her voice, which is the only voice that should tell it.

Je suis enseignante et je dois mener un entretien avec des parents qui ne parlent pas français, avec une interprète. L'entretien porte sur les difficultés de leur fille. Comment bien expliquer dans ces conditions ?

Parlez aux parents, jamais à l'interprète : regardez-les, adressez-vous à leur fille par son prénom, et avancez par phrases courtes et complètes, une idée à la fois. « Amira lit bien à voix haute. C'est comprendre ce qu'elle lit qui lui coûte. Nous avons un plan pour l'aider, et il y a un rôle pour vous à la maison, même sans français. » Des segments courts empêchent l'interprète de résumer — car résumer, c'est déjà décider à la place des parents ce qu'ils doivent entendre.

Commencez par une force réelle de l'enfant avant toute difficulté : dans beaucoup de cultures, une école qui convoque les parents annonce un blâme, et cette première phrase change la nature de la réunion. Puis rendez le plan vérifiable : demandez aux parents de reformuler, par l'interprète, ce qu'ils feront à la maison. Si la reformulation est très courte alors que votre explication était longue, quelque chose s'est perdu — reprenez ce point, autrement.

Enfin, écrivez la consigne essentielle sur papier, dans les deux langues si possible. Une explication orale traverse trois mémoires avant d'arriver à la cuisine familiale ; une phrase écrite n'en traverse aucune.
My cousin moved to the US from a country with public healthcare and set prices. She's bewildered by tipping and by medical bills. I'm her explainer. How do I explain both systems honestly?

Explain each system by its hidden logic, not its surface rules. Tipping first: "In restaurants here, the price on the menu is not the price of the meal — the server's wage is partly paid directly by you, at the end, usually 18 to 20 percent. It's not really a reward for excellence, whatever people say; it's a deferred part of the bill that you're trusted to pay. Refusing it doesn't protest the system, it just docks one person's pay." Then the boundary map: counter service is optional and small, delivery and bars have their own rates, and nobody tips the doctor — which sets up the second system.

Medical bills: "Here the price is the start of a negotiation you never see. The hospital bills one number, the insurer pays a lower, pre-arranged one, and your share depends on your deductible — the amount you pay first each year. The document called an EOB, 'explanation of benefits,' is not a bill; the bill comes separately and should match it. If they don't match, that's normal enough to be worth a phone call, and the call often reduces it."

The kindness in both explanations is the same: tell her which parts are rules, which are customs, and which are negotiable — because a newcomer wastes the most energy treating customs as laws and laws as customs.
My uncle was one of the last lighthouse keepers before automation. At his 80th birthday the grandkids will ask what he did. Help him answer.

He might say: "My job was to make sure the light never lied. Every evening I lit it — in my early years it was an oil lamp I trimmed and wound like a clock — and every hour of the night I checked that it turned with its own rhythm, because ships didn't just use it to find the harbor. They knew which lighthouse it was by how it flashed: two flashes, a pause, two flashes. That pattern was our signature, and if the mechanism slowed, the signature changed, and a captain could mistake us for another rock entirely. In the day I painted, cleaned the lens — a ton of glass prisms worth more than the house — and wrote the weather in the log, every three hours, in ink."

The detail that elevates this from nostalgia to knowledge is the signature: a lighthouse wasn't a lamp, it was an identity in a language of flashes, and the keeper was its proofreader. If a grandchild asks why a machine couldn't do it, let him answer honestly — eventually it could, for the light. What the machine never did was row out to the boat that got it wrong anyway. Keepers were also the rescue service that happened to live on the rock. That sentence, from him, will be the one they repeat at his 90th.
My dad was a cinema projectionist for 40 years. Nobody under 30 knows what that job even was. Write the explanation he can give.

"A film arrived at my cinema as six or seven reels of actual film, heavy as luggage. My job started before yours did: I inspected every reel for tears, spliced the reels together, and threaded the film through the projector — a path of sprockets and loops that had to be exactly right, because the machine pulled twenty-four photographs a second past a lamp hot enough to burn the film if it stopped moving. When a reel ended, I switched to the second projector at the exact frame — that little circle that used to flash in the corner of the screen was my cue mark, my tap on the shoulder. If the film broke, the screen went white, four hundred people looked up at my little window, and I had about ninety seconds of their patience to splice it and restart."

Then the line that gives the trade its dignity: "You never saw my work when it was good. You only saw it when it failed. A projectionist's whole career is four hundred people, twice a night, never once thinking of him."

That last idea — excellence as invisibility — is one the grandchildren will meet in their own jobs, whatever those turn out to be. It's worth his saying plainly, because it's the part of the trade that didn't vanish with the film stock.
Reverse direction: my 15-year-old needs to explain to her grandfather why her friends 'talk all day but never call.' He thinks the group chat is rude and shallow. Give her the explanation.

She can say: "Grandpa, a phone call in your day was like knocking on someone's door — you arrived, all at once, and the person had to stop everything. Our group chat is more like the kitchen table at a house where everyone lives: people wander in, leave a note, answer an hour later, show a photo. Nobody has to stop their day, so nobody minds that it never really ends. The talking looks shallow because you're seeing the kitchen-table layer. The serious conversations still happen one-to-one — they've just moved to private messages, the way you'd have taken someone aside on the porch."

The analogy does the diplomatic work: it maps his world onto hers instead of defending hers as superior. Door-knocking versus kitchen table explains asynchrony — the genuinely new thing — better than any talk of apps. And it concedes his sharpest point in advance: yes, the visible layer is lighter than a call. Elders explaining vanished trades get respect automatically; a teenager explaining a present one has to earn it, and conceding the true part of the criticism first is how she earns the standing to correct the rest.
I do intake at a legal aid clinic, often through interpreters, and clients leave not understanding what happens next in their case. Fix my closing explanation.

Your closing should be a map with three landmarks, delivered slowly, in the client's own frame of time: "Today was step one: we listened and we opened your file. Nothing is decided today. Step two happens in about three weeks: a lawyer — maybe not me — reads everything and decides if we can take the case. We will call you; if your phone number changes, call this number first, because most cases we lose are lost to a changed phone number. Step three: if we take the case, you will get a letter with a date. That date is the one that matters."

Through an interpreter, add two protections. Ask the interpreter beforehand to render the phone-number sentence exactly, not approximately — it's the operational heart of the speech. And end with teach-back: "So I know I explained well — what will you do if you move or change your number?" A client who can answer that owns the one action the whole case depends on.

The deeper fix: clients leave confused because intake explanations describe the institution (departments, review committees, eligibility criteria) instead of the client's experience (waiting, being called, one date). Explain the institution's process only as it touches them, in the order it touches them, with their own duties named in the same breath as yours.

My great-aunt sent telegrams and worked the telegraph office as a young woman. She's writing her memories for the family. How should she explain the telegraph to descendants who've only known instant messages?

Suggest she start with the price, because price explains everything about the form: "You paid by the word, so nobody wrote 'I am writing to tell you that I will arrive on Tuesday.' You wrote ARRIVING TUESDAY STOP — and I was the one who turned your words into dots and dashes, and turned other people's dots and dashes back into words, at forty words a minute, by ear. The wire hummed in code all day and I read it the way you read print."

Then the part that makes her a witness, not just an operator: telegrams were how the twentieth century delivered its extremes — war deaths, births, offers of marriage, fortunes lost — and they all arrived through a human being who typed them, sealed them, and sent a boy on a bicycle. People feared the sight of the telegram boy the way later generations feared a knock from a uniform. She was the face of other people's best and worst days.

The bridge for her descendants: their instant messages are free and therefore endless; hers cost money per word and therefore every telegram is a haiku written by necessity. Brevity wasn't a style. It was arithmetic. Have her include one real telegram, if the family kept any — a single line of it teaches more than a chapter about the technology.

Acabamos de mudarnos a este país y no entiendo el sistema escolar: hablan de primaria, secundaria, créditos y distritos. ¿Me lo explicas como a un padre que solo quiere saber dónde encaja su hijo de 12 años?

Claro, empecemos por su hijo y luego abramos el mapa. Con 12 años, su hijo entra en la etapa intermedia: ya no está con un solo maestro todo el día, sino que cambia de aula y de profesor según la materia. Esa es la gran diferencia que notará la primera semana.

El sistema se divide en tres pisos: la primaria, donde un maestro acompaña al grupo casi todo el día; la intermedia, que es el puente — varios maestros, más independencia, y por eso suele costar el primer trimestre —; y la secundaria, donde aparecen los créditos: cada asignatura aprobada suma puntos, y al final se necesita un total para graduarse. Piense en los créditos como una cuenta que se va llenando durante cuatro años.

El distrito es simplemente la zona escolar: el barrio donde vive decide, por defecto, a qué escuelas públicas puede ir su hijo. Por eso el primer papel que le pedirán en todas partes es un comprobante de domicilio.

Su tarea este mes es solo una: inscribirlo con ese comprobante y pedir la reunión de bienvenida. Lo demás — optativas, deportes, niveles — se decide después, con el tutor, y se lo explicarán paso a paso. Un sistema nuevo se aprende puerta a puerta, no de golpe.
I'm releasing a small open-source command-line tool that renames photo files by date. Write the first paragraph of my README — the one that decides whether anyone reads further.

Here's your paragraph: "photodate renames the chaos in your photo folders — IMG_4021.jpg, DSC_0093.jpg — into names that sort themselves: 2024-06-15_143022.jpg, using the date each photo was actually taken. Point it at a folder and it works on copies by default, so your originals are never at risk. It handles JPEG and PNG, runs offline, and asks before overwriting anything."

Why it's built this way: the first sentence opens with the reader's mess, not your technology — nobody searches for a renaming tool in the abstract; they search because a folder looks like that. The second sentence contains the two facts that decide adoption for a tool that touches irreplaceable files: what it produces, and that it can't hurt them. "Works on copies by default" is doing more for your download count than any feature list below it.

What the paragraph must not contain: your implementation language, your motivation story, and the word "simple" — readers decide simplicity for themselves, and the ones burned by other tools read "simple" as a warning. Installation comes next, and it should be one command, because the first paragraph made a promise the second must keep cheaply.
I'm a night nurse writing the handover note for the day shift. Our notes are either novels or useless. Write me a model note for a typical patient and tell me the rules it follows.

Model note: "Bed 12, Mrs. Alvarez, 68, post-op day 2, hip replacement. Night quiet overall. Pain 4/10 at 02:00, settled to 2 after scheduled meds — she's been under-reporting, ask her directly. Ate nothing, drank well. First walk at 06:00 with physio: managed 10 metres, keen to do more. Watch: temp 37.8 at 05:00, up from 37.2 — no other signs, but recheck at 08:00 before it becomes a story. Daughter visits at 10:00, anxious, wants to speak to the surgeon. Catheter out, voiding fine."

The rules it follows: lead with identity and trajectory in one line, so a nurse taking six patients can sort priorities before reading details. Report changes, not states — the day shift can read the chart for baselines; what only you know is what moved overnight. Give numbers where numbers exist and flag the one trend that matters with its next check time, so vigilance has a schedule. Include the human logistics (the anxious daughter at 10:00) because the day shift's hardest moments are rarely clinical. And write nothing you wouldn't want read aloud at the bedside — handover notes have a way of traveling. A note that follows these rules runs six lines and outperforms the novel, because the novel's reader skims, and skimming is where handovers actually fail.
I volunteer at a farming museum and I have exactly 60 words for the label next to a seed drill. Write it, and show me your word count discipline.

Here is the label, at 58 words:

"Seed Drill, c. 1880. Before this machine, farmers scattered seed by hand from a bag — much of it eaten by birds or buried too deep. The drill's tubes drop seeds in neat rows at an even depth, so more grain grows from less seed. Jethro Tull designed the first in 1701; this one fed a family farm."

The discipline: spend the first sentence on identity and date, because that's the label's contract. The middle goes to the before — a visitor can't value a solution without the problem, and broadcasting seed by hand is a scene anyone can picture. One sentence of mechanism, in verbs a child owns (drop, grow), no word like "metering mechanism." The last sentence returns to scale: a named inventor for the curious, then the human unit — one family farm — because visitors remember who used a thing longer than how it worked. Every draft of a museum label should be cut by asking of each sentence: if the visitor reads only this one, do they leave with something true? Words beyond sixty are rarely information; they're the writer's reluctance to choose.
We sell a flat-pack bookshelf and our assembly instructions keep generating returns from people who build it backwards. Rewrite the first page of instructions for a tired stranger at 9 p.m.

First page, rewritten:

"BEFORE YOU START: You need a screwdriver and 40 minutes. Build it on the floor, on the cardboard, so nothing scratches. Lay out all parts. You should have: 2 tall sides, 4 shelves, 1 back panel, 1 bag of screws.

STEP 1 — THE ONLY STEP YOU CAN GET WRONG: The two tall sides are not identical. Find the side with holes along BOTH edges. It goes on your LEFT, holes facing IN. Put a piece of tape on it now and write LEFT. Done? Everything after this is easy."

The design principles: write for the reader's actual state — tired, on the floor, mildly annoyed — not for the engineer who designed the shelf. The returns told you where the failure lives (the mirrored sides), so the instructions spend their sternest words there, before any damage, instead of distributing warnings evenly like a legal document. The tape trick converts an abstract orientation into a physical mark that survives the whole build; a reader who marked LEFT cannot build it backwards in step 6, which is where your old instructions were still pleading. Finally, inventory before assembly: discovering a missing shelf at step 1 is an inconvenience; at step 7 it's a return.
Our dev team has an internal script that rebuilds the test database. New joiners are scared to run it. Write the opening of its README.

"This script rebuilds your local test database from scratch: it wipes the test database on your own machine and recreates it with sample data, in about two minutes. It cannot touch production — it checks the database name and refuses to run against anything that isn't called test. Run it whenever your local data gets into a weird state; you cannot break anything that isn't already disposable. If it fails halfway, run it again — it's safe to repeat."

Fear of a tool is usually fear of one unspecified catastrophe, so the opening spends most of its words fencing off the catastrophe precisely: what it wipes (your local test data), what it cannot do (production, guarded by name), and what failure costs (nothing — run it again). Notice it answers the questions a scared person actually asks, in their order: What does it destroy? Can it hurt anything real? What if it goes wrong? The usage syntax comes after, because nobody reads flags while frightened.

The general rule for internal docs: the first paragraph of a tool's README is a safety briefing disguised as an introduction. Teams that write it that way get tools that get used; teams that open with architecture get tools that one person runs and everyone else routes around.
I run an auto shop. The closing tech writes handover notes for the morning crew like 'blue Honda still making noise.' Write a model note and the standard it sets.

Model note: "2019 Accord, plate ending 4417, ticket 88 — the rattle. Reproduced it on the lift: noise is the loose exhaust heat shield at the rear, not the suspension. Shield bolts are rusted; I soaked them, didn't force them. Morning job: heat and remove, replace shield if it tears. Customer approved up to $200 by phone at 17:40, she needs the car by 15:00 for a school run. Loaner keys are in the red box if it runs long. — D."

The standard it sets: identify the vehicle three ways (model, plate fragment, ticket) because "blue Honda" describes two cars on any given night. Report the diagnosis as a finding, including the dead end ruled out — "not the suspension" saves the morning tech an hour of re-diagnosis and is the single most valuable sentence in the note. State what state you left things in (bolts soaked, not forced), what authorization exists and its ceiling, the customer's real deadline and its reason, and the contingency already arranged. Sign it: unsigned notes can't be questioned, and a note that can't be questioned will eventually be a note nobody trusts. The morning crew doesn't need more notes; it needs notes written as if the writer had to receive them.
Je tiens un petit musée local et je dois écrire l'étiquette d'un poste de radio des années 1940. Soixante mots maximum. Écris-la-moi.

Voici l'étiquette, en 59 mots :

« Poste de radio, vers 1942. Avant la télévision, cette boîte en bois était la fenêtre du village sur le monde. Chaque soir, la famille s'asseyait autour pour écouter les nouvelles, la météo des moissons et, pendant la guerre, les messages codés destinés à la Résistance. Il fallait attendre que les lampes chauffent : la patience faisait partie du rituel. »

Le choix des informations suit une règle simple : d'abord ce que c'est et quand, ensuite la scène de vie qui le rend réel — la famille assise autour —, puis le détail que le visiteur ne devinera jamais seul. Ici, c'est le temps de chauffe des lampes : un détail technique minuscule qui dit tout d'une époque où l'information demandait de l'attente. Les messages codés donnent l'enjeu historique sans transformer l'étiquette en cours d'histoire. Remarquez ce qui a été sacrifié : la marque, la technique des ondes, la fréquence. Soixante mots obligent à choisir, et le bon choix est presque toujours la vie autour de l'objet plutôt que l'objet lui-même.
Our water filter cartridges come with instructions that people ignore, then they call us when the water tastes bad. Write the replacement instructions that survive real life.

The card that goes in the box:

"TIME TO CHANGE THE FILTER? (Every 6 months — write today's date on the new one.)
1. Turn the blue tap on the filter OFF. If you skip this, step 3 is a fountain.
2. Twist the white case a quarter-turn left. It will drip a little — that's normal, use the towel.
3. Drop the old cartridge in the bin. Put the new one in with the rubber ring UP.
4. Twist right until it clicks. Turn the blue tap back ON.
5. Run the cold tap for 2 minutes. The water will look cloudy, then clear. That cloudiness is harmless air, not dirt.
Done. If it still tastes odd after a day, call us: 555-0134."

Every line answers a known failure. The date-writing is moved to the top because the real instruction isn't mechanical — it's remembering in six months. Step 1 names its own consequence, because warnings without consequences get skipped. Step 5 pre-explains the cloudy water, which is the single largest source of your support calls: an unexplained surprise reads as a defect. And the whole card assumes the reader is under a sink, on their knees, in poor light — short lines, big verbs, no paragraph longer than a breath. Instructions don't fail because people are careless; they fail because they were written for a reader sitting at a desk that doesn't exist.
I open a bakery at 4 a.m. and my evening baker leaves me chaotic notes. Show me what a good closing handover note looks like so I can pin it up as the example.

Pin this one up: "Tuesday close. Ovens off, gas checked. For the morning: sourdough is in the retard, second shelf — it's lively, it will be ready to shape by 5, don't let it go past 6. Croissant dough is one fold short; butter was warm today. We're out of rye flour — order is due Thursday, so Wednesday's menu drops the rye loaf; sign is already in the drawer. The good eggs are at the back of the walk-in, the front tray is for scrambling only. Mrs. Chen's birthday cake order moved to Friday — she called at 20:00, confirmed. Cooler is running 1 degree warm, logged it, watching. — P."

What makes it good enough to pin up: it's ordered by the reader's morning, not the writer's evening — the first things the opener must act on come first, with their deadlines attached (shape by 5, not past 6). Deviations from normal get reasons in four words ("butter was warm today"), because a note that says what without why forces the morning baker to guess whether it matters. Substitutions and shortages arrive with the decision already made (rye dropped, sign ready), sparing the 4 a.m. brain a menu decision. And the small ominous item — the warm cooler — is present, logged, and sized. A handover note is a letter to a colleague who will read it half-awake and alone; write to that reader.
Our town museum got the first telephone installed in the county, from 1911. Write its label — 60 words max — for visitors who've never used a phone with a cord.

The label, at 56 words:

"Telephone, 1911 — the first in the county, installed in Hartley's General Store. It has no dial and no numbers: you turned the crank, and an operator in the exchange connected you by hand. Calls were semi-public events, made standing in the store, and most were short. Within ten years, forty farms had joined the line."

Writing for visitors who've never touched a corded phone means explaining absences, which is harder than explaining features. The label spends its words on the two absences that change everything: no dial (so a human intermediary stood inside every call) and no privacy (so the telephone entered life as a public instrument, not a personal one — the opposite of the phone in the visitor's pocket). "Standing in the store" is the scene that carries it: one image corrects a century of assumptions. The closing number gives the adoption curve in a single breath, and note what's omitted — the manufacturer, the magneto mechanism. At sixty words, a label is an act of triage, and the social facts almost always outrank the mechanical ones for a general visitor.
I work for a car rental company. Our after-hours return instructions confuse everyone and cars end up in the wrong lot. Rewrite them.

"RETURNING AFTER HOURS — 3 minutes, 4 steps.
1. Park in LOT B — the one with the yellow lines, behind the office. (Lot A is staff parking; cars left there can't be checked in.)
2. Note your mileage and fuel level on the card in the glovebox.
3. Lock the car. Put the keys AND the card in the drop box by the office door — the silver box, it clunks when it closes.
4. Take a photo of the parked car. It's your proof and ours.
Your rental ends when the keys hit the box, not when we open it — you won't be charged for the night."

The original presumably failed the way most such instructions fail: it described the process from the company's side (check-in procedures, inspection order) instead of the customer's path through the dark in the rain. Every rewrite choice here answers a real failure: the lots are distinguished by what the driver can see (yellow lines) plus the consequence of the wrong one, given once, in parentheses. The clunk is specified because a silent box leaves people rattling it and doubting. And the last line resolves the anxiety that makes customers phone at midnight — when does the meter stop? Instructions for strangers in the dark should be written as if read by torchlight, in weather, by someone whose flight is at six. Most are written for a person who doesn't exist, in an office that isn't theirs.
I'm writing the intro to our team's data-cleaning checklist for new analysts. They follow the steps but don't understand why, so they skip steps when rushed. Write the opening.

"Every dataset that reaches this checklist has already lied to someone. The steps below exist because each one has caught a real lie: the duplicate customer who doubled a revenue figure in a board report (step 2), the dates stored as text that silently dropped a month from an analysis (step 4), the 'Other' category that hid a product line for a quarter (step 6). Clean in the order given — later checks assume earlier ones passed. When you're rushed, this checklist is the last thing to cut: an hour of cleaning is cheaper than one wrong number in a room where decisions get made, because the wrong number is never the one that gets questioned. It looks exactly like the right ones."

The opening treats skipped steps as an explanation failure, not a discipline failure — which is correct. A step whose purpose is invisible will be rationally skipped by any busy person, so each step is introduced by the incident that created it. Rules with biographies get followed; rules without them get triaged. Notice too that it argues from the analyst's own interest: the person who ships the wrong number owns it publicly, while the hour of cleaning is anonymous. If your analysts understand that the checklist is armor for them, not bureaucracy for you, the rushing problem mostly solves itself.
Voy a cuidar el perro de mi vecina una semana y me dejó una nota larguísima y desordenada. ¿Cómo sería la nota perfecta para cuidar a un perro ajeno?

La nota perfecta sería breve, ordenada por el día del perro y no por las preocupaciones de la dueña:

«BRUNO — la semana en una hoja.
Comida: una taza a las 7:00 y otra a las 18:00, del saco azul. Nada de comida de humanos: el queso le sienta mal.
Paseos: mañana y noche, 20 minutos. Tira de la correa si ve gatos; sujeta fuerte y cruza la calle.
Casa: duerme en su manta de la cocina. Si hay tormenta, se asusta: déjale la radio puesta.
Salud: su pastilla va dentro de un trozo de salchicha, con la cena. Si no come dos comidas seguidas o lo ves raro, llama a la clínica: 555-2210, pregunta por la ficha de Bruno.
Emergencias: mi móvil está en la nevera. La vecina de enfrente tiene llave. ¡Gracias!»

Fíjese en el orden: primero lo que ocurre todos los días y a qué hora, porque quien cuida consulta la nota con el perro ya ladrando. Después, los problemas conocidos con su solución ya decidida — el queso, los gatos, la tormenta —, porque una advertencia sin instrucción («cuidado con los gatos») deja al cuidador solo justo en el momento difícil. La salud va al final pero con el criterio de alarma escrito: no «si está enfermo», sino la señal concreta que debe buscar. Y la nota cabe en una hoja, porque una nota de cuatro páginas no se relee jamás; la perfecta no es la que más dice, sino la que se encuentra rápido a las dos de la mañana.
Final test of my instruction-writing course: rewrite a tent setup guide for two tired people arriving at a campsite in fading light. Show me what the course has been teaching.

"STOP. Before anything: put the tent bag down and eat something if you haven't. A tent pitched hungry takes twice as long.

1. Find your ground first: flat, and not in a dip — if it rains, dips become ponds. Lie down on it. Your body is the best level you own.
2. Lay the tent body out and peg the four corners loosely. Don't tighten anything yet.
3. Build the two poles on the ground beside the tent. They're identical — if one seems longer, you've missed a section; they always come apart in your hands, not in the tent.
4. Push each pole through its sleeve, then — together, one person each end — lift both arches at the same moment and seat the ends in the corner rings. This is the only step that needs two people and daylight. Everything after can be done by torch.
5. Clip the tent to the poles, working from the middle out. Throw the rain cover over, and only now tighten the corner pegs.
6. The test: push the tent from the side. It should push back. If a corner lifts, that peg goes deeper, at an angle away from the tent."

Everything the course taught is in there. Sequence by dependency and by light — the daylight-critical step is identified and front-loaded, because the reader's real deadline is the sun, not the tent. Errors are pre-named at the moment they occur (the pole that "seems longer," the dip that becomes a pond), which converts panic into recognition. Two-person work is flagged before it's attempted solo. And the closing test replaces inspection-by-checklist with a physical verification a tired person can trust. Instructions are a form of explanation under the worst conditions — fatigue, weather, failing light — and a guide that survives those has nothing left to fear from a rested reader at a desk.
